subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS, QUEBEC- MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS, QUEBEC- MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, March 2 I was questioned in the' house concerning the meeting held in Quebec city on Saturday, February 29, on the subject of the administration of services for Eskimos in northern Quebec.
Present at the meeting in Quebec city on behalf of the province of Quebec were Hon. Rene Levesque and Hon. Claire Kirkland-Casgrain, and present representing the federal government besides myself were the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
Last Monday I stated to the house that a report of the discussions was being made to
the cabinet and thereafter might be announced in the house. With the permission of the house I am now in a position to table the understanding reached at the February 29 meeting, and I may say that the same information is being made available by the provincial authorities in Quebec city today. I am tabling two copies of the memorandum of understanding in English and two copies in French. Perhaps if it met the wishes of hon. members, Mr. Speaker, the memorandum, which runs to just over a page, might be printed as an annex to today's Hansard, to save the time of the house at this stage and to provide for easy reference.
The memorandum is not an agreement, nor is it an agreement to agree. It does constitute a statement outlining a consensus with respect to certain basic principles and conditions which, in the event of an agreement, are common to the two governments. Provision is made to refer these principles and conditions to a joint committee of federal and provincial officials who are charged with the responsibility of preparing a draft agreement, as well as the terms of reference for the commission which will be asked to receive the views and comments of the Eskimos.
The Eskimos will be consulted through a commission appointed jointly by the federal and provincial governments, and no agreement will be concluded with the province of Quebec until this is done. I am satisfied that the principles embodied in the memorandum of understanding fully protect the essential interests of the Eskimos. I would like to add, Mr. Speaker, only that the discussions with the Quebec ministers were constructive, and that a good foundation has been laid for a thorough examination in the coming days of the many matters involved.

maintopic: TABLING OP REPORT OF SAINT JOHN RIVER BOARD

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: TABLING OP REPORT OF SAINT JOHN RIVER BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to advise that the governments of Canada and of New Brunswick have agreed to the release as a public document of the report "Effects of storage on power generation in New Brunswick" and I take this opportunity to table a copy of this report.
This report was prepared by the Saint John river board established jointly by the two governments on March 24, 1959. The board consisted of two members each from Canada and from New Brunswick, and was asked by the two governments to:
-plan, supervise and carry out an investigation to determine how the present and future power developments in New Brunswick would he affected by the development and operation of storage on the upper Saint John river and its tributaries.
I am pleased to state that the Canadian members of this board were two members of the staff of the water resources branch of my department.
The board presented its report to the two governments in June, 1960 and since that time the report has been used by New Brunswick in its planning and development of the Saint John river for power generation purposes. The report is now being made public because its contents may be useful to other public and private agencies concerned with integrated river development. In particular it may be useful to those participating in the technical talks between Canada and the United States relative to the Passamaquoddy tidal power project and the upper Saint John river in Maine.
The findings of the Saint John river board report which are of interprovincial and international importance are summarized as follows:
(a)	The power potential of the Saint John river in New Brunswick would be economical without upstream storage at Rankin rapids and without an energy interchange with Nova Scotia.

(b)	An energy exchange with Nova Scotia designed to give maximum system economy would accelerate the development of this power potential.
(c)	Small potential storages on tributaries of the Saint John river would have a limited benefit to the power development in systems where no storage was developed at the Rankin rapids site.
(d)	The development of the Rankin rapids storage while not affecting the ultimate installed capacity at downstream plants would provide temporary capacity benefits and continuing energy benefits to power developments on the Saint John river in New Brunswick. The inclusion of the Passamaquoddy project would have a negligible effect on these benefits.
(e)	Co-ordination of the New Brunswick and Nova Scotia power systems with utilities in Maine would produce monetary savings, particularly in the period up to 1980.
I regret that the supply of copies of this report is not sufficient to provide them to individual members. However, they will be able to have access to it among the papers of the house, and in the meantime I am having a summary of the report prepared in ample quantity for those desiring copies.

maintopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF NELSON RIVER PROGRAMMING BOARD

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF NELSON RIVER PROGRAMMING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement at this time on the preliminary studies of the electric power potential of the Nelson river which have been carried out by the Nelson river programming board under the agreement of February 18, 1963, between the governments of Canada and Manitoba.
In entering this agreement the government of Canada had regard to several factors, among which were these:
(1)	The government was aware that a large potential for hydro power existed on the Nelson river in northern Manitoba.
(2)	That the potential for power production was much greater than the growing southern Manitoba markets could absorb for many years to come.
(3)	That large power markets probably existed in southern Ontario and in the north central United States which might be interested in obtaining substantial sources of power supply.
(4)	That the trend in capital costs of hydro developments could have the effect of pricing undeveloped sites out of the power market of the future.
(5)	That development and delivery of Nelson river power to southern Manitoba or other distant markets at rates competitive with
Nelson River Board Report alternative sources would entail large units of installation to permit the advantages of economy of scale.
(6)	That the preliminary investigations undertaken at an estimated cost of $1 million equally shared between Canada and Manitoba were designed to determine the merits of proceeding with more comprehensive and detailed studies.
I am pleased to be able to report that a great deal of engineering and geological field work as well as preliminary electrical system studies have now been completed, and the Nelson river programming board has just submitted its interim report to the government of Canada and the government of Manitoba.
In brief, the report indicates that there is a hydraulic power potential in excess of 4 million kilowatts on the Nelson river, and that on the basis of current rates of market development in Manitoba, approximately 2 million kilowatts will be surplus to Manitoba's requirements for perhaps 25 years. The preliminary studies confirmed the availability of power sites which are eminently suited for development, and revealed on site and delivered power costs which are very encouraging and which indicate the possibility of substantial blocks of Nelson river power being able to reach the markets of southern Ontario and the north-central United States at competitive rates.
The development of a major source of low cost hydroelectric power in Manitoba would clearly have important effects on neighbouring provinces and on the over-all national power picture. If a major block of Nelson river power is exported outside of Canada or to southern Manitoba, it will appreciably improve our balance of payments situation with the United States.
In view of these general considerations and the findings contained in the board report, the government of Canada is now prepared to enter into discussions with the government of Manitoba with a view to arriving at satisfactory arrangements for the next stage of more detailed studies of the Nelson river power development program.
I would now ask permission of the house to table the interim report of the Nelson river programming board.

I think it is more than coincidence that this statement should be made during the time we are discussing the Columbia river, because the decision that was made to undertake this study in co-operation with the government of Manitoba concerning the power potential of the Nelson river was a part of the broad overall national policy of developing the resources of Canada as quickly as possible. subtopic: DEPARTMENTAL RESEARCH INTO USES FOR BUTTERFAT
DEPARTMENTAL RESEARCH INTO USES FOR BUTTERFAT
speechtext: What research has been conducted by the research branch of the Department of Agriculture with a view to discovering new uses for butterfat, and if any, when, and with what result?

subtopic: DEPARTMENTAL RESEARCH INTO USES FOR BUTTERFAT
speechtext:
The wider use of butterfat is under continuous consideration by the food research institute, research branch. Work has been aimed largely at improving the acceptability of butterfat. During the past five years this has embraced studies of the chemical compounds that contribute the flavour to butter, of the flavour stability of butter oil in consumer packages, and of the plastic range of butter, i.e., spreadability.

speechtext:
1.	What are the postal regulations which provide for a salary reduction for employees for mistakes or poor work, and (a) when were these passed (b) how much are these pay reductions (c) has the department considered suspension rather than pay reductions?
2.	Is second class mail, such as magazines, delivered on special days even if letter carriers are required to work overtime to make such deliveries and, if so (a) under what regulation is this done (b) what officials of the Post Office Department have the authority to give such orders (c) are postal employees paid overtime for such extra work?

maintopic: P.O. DEPARTMENT  PENALTIES FOR POOR WORK   SECOND CLASS MAIL DELIVERY
speechtext:
1. The penalties which the Post Office Department imposes on employees for repeated mistakes or habitual poor work are authorized by the Civil Service Act. This act gives all deputies the authority to recommend to the civil service commission penalties, when necessary, in the form of withholding statutory salary increases, salary reduction, demotion in class, suspension, dismissal. (a) The present Civil Service Act came into force on April 1, 1962. (b) The amount of the pay reductions varies according to the circumstances, from a reduction in salary of $5 for one month to $10 per month for six months, and in a few cases more severe penalties in the form of a reduction to a lower step in the established range for the particular class, (c) Yes. Several years ago the most common type of penalty was suspension. This was reviewed with the department's staff associations and the present

system of temporary pay reduction was adopted in preference to the previous practice.
2. (a) Mail is handled in accordance with the service requirements established for each class of mail. Magazine companies publishing dated material try to schedule their delivery to the post office in order that the publications will be available for delivery on a certain day each week or month, as the case may be. Notwithstanding the foregoing, second class mail does not take precedence over first class mail, nor is it customary for letter carriers to work overtime on any day, to make deliveries of second class mail.
Letter carriers work a five day, 40 hour week and their routes are so constituted as to enable delivery, on the average, within the eight hour workday prescribed by the department. Each route is verified by means of a periodic check and if found to require adjustment to bring it within the prescribed work week, such adjustment is made. In addition, if any letter carrier feels that his route is too heavy or has increased in volume, he has the right to apply for an additional work check and if his claim is substantiated, he is given an overtime award until such time as an adjustment can be made, (b) Only senior officers at headquarters can authorize overtime for letter carriers, apart from that mentioned in 2 (a), (c) Letter carriers are not paid overtime for occasional days, unless it has been specifically authorized by the senior officers referred to in 2 (b). It is realized that on occasional days a letter carrier may work beyond the usual time to complete his work, but this is generally more than made up on those days when the volume of mail is less and the letter carrier completes his work early.

1.	Is Canada a member of the International Labour Organization and, if so, who are Canada's representatives on that organization?
2.	Did Canada vote in Geneva on interdicting the South African government and preventing it from taking part in the general conference of that organization and, if so, how did Canada vote and upon what grounds was the Canadian decision made?

1. Yes. The Canadian
government representative on the governing body is Mr. George V. Haythorne, deputy minister of labour.
2. The governing body which met in Geneva earlier this month decided to place on the 48th session of the conference next June three items concerning South Africa:
(1)	Proposed declaration concerning the policy of apartheid of the Republic of South Africa together with a proposed I.L.O. program for the elimination of apartheid in labour matters, dealing with South African legislation and policies in respect of equality of opportunity in respect of admission to employment and training, freedom from forced labour, and freedom of association and the right to organize;
(2)	inclusion in the constitution of the International Labour Organization of a provision empowering the conference to expel or suspend from membership any member which has been expelled or suspended from membership of the United Nations; and
(3)	exclusion in the constitution of the International Labour Organization of a provision empowering the conference to suspend from participation in the international labour conference any member which has been found by the United Nations to be flagrantly and persistently pursuing by its legislation a declared policy of racial discrimination such as apartheid.
The proposals to place the first two items on the agenda of the conference were approved unanimously by the governing body. The proposal concerning the third item was approved by 32 votes in favour, 14 against and two abstentions. Canada was one of eight governments voting against this proposal.
Canada supported the proposed declaration and program for the elimination of apartheid

in labour matters as offering a constructive approach to the apartheid problem within the I.L.O.'s terms of reference.
Although the Canadian government is opposed to the idea of the expulsion of any member from the United Nations or from UN agencies at the present time, the Canadian representative supported the first of the two proposals for the amendment of the I.L.O. constitution because it recognized the principle that the question of expulsion of a member country from the I.L.O. or from any of the UN specialized agencies is primarily a political matter on which the agencies should not take action unless the United Nations had previously taken similar action. Canada opposed the second proposed constitutional amendment because this amendment does not recognize this principle and because of our belief that if South Africa were suspended from participation in the international labour conference it would be more difficult to implement the proposed I.L.O. program for the elimination of apartheid, which calls for the co-operation of the South African government.

maintopic: * ATTENDANCE OF CANADIANS AT INNSBRUCK CONFERENCE
* ATTENDANCE OF CANADIANS AT INNSBRUCK CONFERENCE
speechtext:
1.	How many top ranking Canadian external affairs officials attended the Innsbruck conference?
2.	What positions do those said officials hold with the Department of External Affairs and had they had any special training in reference to European affairs, and in particular, special knowledge of the winter games and, if so, what special knowledge had they?
3.	What top ranking cabinet minister attended the said conference, and how many sessions, days and hours was the minister present?
4.	Was a special brief presented by the Canadian government at the session in reference to the merits that Banff had to offer as an Olympic site?
5.	For what reason did the minister of external affairs not attend the conference in view of the importance of Canada's success at the conference?
6.	What money was spent by the Canadian government in preparing and sending the delegation to the conference?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: * ATTENDANCE OF CANADIANS AT INNSBRUCK CONFERENCE
speechtext:
1, 2, and 3. By the "Innsbruck conference" it is presumed that reference is made to the meeting of the international Olympic committee which was held in Innsbruck during the period January 25-28, 1964, and at which the international Olympic committee selected the site for the staging of the 1968 Olympic winter games.
In accordance with the rules of the international Olympic committee, Olympic games are awarded to a city, not to a country, and invitations to stage Olympic games must come from the mayor or highest authority of the city.
The international Olympic committee meetings are only attended by members of the committee; these are private citizens. Occasionally members of international sports of federations and representatives of national Olympic associations attend these meetings by special invitation, but government representatives are never invited to attend the international Olympic committee sessions.

For the foregoing reasons no officials of the Department of External Affairs or any Canadian federal government department attended the meeting of the international Olympic committee. However the Canadian federal government was officially represented at the 1964 Olympic winter games which were held at Innsbruck from January 29 to February 9 inclusive, subsequent to the international Olympic committee meeting. The Hon. Judy LaMarsh attended the official opening ceremony and a number of other events as personal representative of the Prime Minister and as minister responsible for the administration of the national fitness and amateur sport program. Miss M. Meagher, Canadian ambassador to Austria, represented the Canadian government at Innsbruck during the games.
4.	An application to stage the 1968 Olympic winter games in Banff, Alberta, was presented to the international Olympic committee on January 28 by an official delegation, headed by the mayor of Calgary, who was assisted by Mr. James Worrall, president of the Canadian Olympic association, Mr. Ed. Davis, president of the Calgary Olympic development association, Mr. Hans Maciej, vice president of the Calgary Olympic development association, and Mr. J. H. Messinger, general manager of the Calgary Olympic development association. The Calgary application to stage the 1968 Olympic winter games in Banff had the full support of the federal government. However no special briefs or representations were made by the Canadian federal government with reference to the merits of Banff as such action is not permitted under the rules of the international Olympic committee.
5.	See answers 1, 2, and 3 above.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs and his department have at all times given appropriate assistance to the sponsors of the Calgary application.
6.	The promotional costs of preparing Calgary's application to stage the 1968 Olympic winter games in Banff were shared by the federal, provincial and municipal governments, with a portion of the funds coming from private sources. The Canadian federal government spent a total of $110,000 in grants for the years 1961-1963 inclusive to assist the Calgary Olympic development associ-tion in all the aspects of preparing its application, which included the costs of sending the official Calgary delegation to Innsbruck. The federal grants were matched by the province of Alberta, and the city of Calgary, and by private groups and citizens.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State. In view of the urgent interest in the matter, can the Secretary of State inform the house with regard to the status of the charter of the Hett clinic foundation in Windsor, in the

Inquiries of the Ministry light of statements made by Dr. Cotnam, supervising coroner of Ontario, as found in this morning's Globe and Mail?

subtopic: WINDSOR
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CLOSING OF HETT FOUNDATION
speechtext:
Before answering this question I should like to say that I have also received from the hon. member for Simcoe East notice of his intention to ask a similar question. This matter arises out of a coroner's inquest into the death of Donald McConnell, which occurred at the clinic in Windsor operated by this foundation. The foundation is a federal company incorporated under part II of the Companies Act in 1947.
The coroner's jury in its findings recommended that the charter for this clinic be revoked, and a copy of these findings was forwarded to the Department of the Secretary of State by Dr. Cotnam asking merely for the department's comments.
Under the Companies Act there is no provision whereby the charter of a dominion part II corporation may be revoked by simple fiat of the Secretary of State, even though there is a recommendation by a coroner's jury. The procedure is at common law before the courts of the province where the corporation is doing business. To proceed in this fashion would require a complete investigation of the operations of this foundation, which normally would be instigated by the provincial authorities.
The department of the attorney general of Ontario has been asked to bring to the attention of my department any further developments in the situation and has been invited to make any other recommendations which it may care to make at this time.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, March 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Martin (Essex East):
That the treaty between Canada and the United States of America relating to co-operative development of the water resources of the Columbia river basin, signed at Washington on January 17, 1961, together with the protocol containing modifications and clarifications to the treaty annexed to an exchange of notes between the governments of Canada and the United States signed on January 22, 1964, be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to continue my remarks, there are several points which have been laboured by the critics of the Columbia river treaty, particularly by certain members of the New Democratic party. It is to me most disturbing, yes, tragic, to hear the leader of that party say that he will do everything within his power to block the passage of the protocol, and the treaty's ratification. May I say to the hon. member that his task will be as formidable as would be that of turning back the hands of time.
The people of Canada, particularly in British Columbia, of the Kootenay and the Columbia areas, yes even of Kootenay West and Burnaby-Coquitlam, are intelligent enough to recognize a bargain when they see one, and what is for their own benefit. To say that it really is a betrayal of Canadian interest is foolish prattle and certainly something which is not true. It is to be noted, among several points which I think are important enough to be brought up here, that not one kilowatt of actual power generated in Canada is to be exported to the United States. The only power to be sold is that power which will be generated in the United States as a result of dams built in Canada, and this extra power will be shared according to the terms of the treaty. This is actually the sale of a service. It is not the export, and not the sale of power.
A great deal has been said about depleting the water supply of the west which might ultimately be used for purposes of irrigation on the prairies. As I mentioned at the beginning of my speech, the headwaters of most of these rivers that we are talking about begin on the western border of my constituency. I happen to know all of these rivers well, and that the real source of the supply of water for the prairies, should it ever be needed, as far as the economic aspect is concerned, is not the Columbia. It is the Clearwater; it is the Brazeau; it is the Red Deer, it is even the Athabaska; because to divert

some of the waters of these rivers for irrigation purposes on to the prairies would be far cheaper than to divert the waters of the Columbia, and certainly the supply is such that there is no question as to the quantity of water.
There is another aspect of this that is important. As a result of the sale of downstream benefits there will be money sufficient to pay for the construction of the entire project within Canada. How much more would the cost of this project be to the taxpayers of Canada if we were to try to finance it ourselves? Actually it would be more than double the cost of the initial construction, because the way we finance such public service today, the cost of the money is far more than the cost of the actual project itself. So, I maintain and I think it is a very logical conclusion that the benefit of this Columbia river project is not just in terms of dollars, not just in terms of kilowatt hours of power, but it represents long term benefits which must be included if we are to look at the over-all picture.
There has been talk about the uncertainty of the cost of these projects. I would just remind hon. members of this house that the British Columbia government has already spent some $10 million in feasibility surveys and essential initial preparation. So when you look at it from these different aspects you see that in addition to the dollars and cents benefits that were outlined yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, there are many other additional benefits which enter into the picture and which make this, as far as any business proposition is concerned, a mighty good bargain.
I do not want to talk very much longer on this treaty, least of all do I want to delve into matters of great technical detail when the very motion before the house is to refer such matters to their proper committee where witnesses can be examined and all sides of the story told. Everyone in this house knows perfectly well that it is possible to put up a plausible story to cover either side one may take on this question. The government and official opposition have in fact had the unusual opportunity to argue on both sides of the question and I am sure they realize this full well.
The only place we are going to get the answers we need is in the committee, and technical matters have little place in discussions on the floor of the house at this time. The only technical matters that are perfectly obvious to me are, first, that while politicians talk, the Columbia river continues to flow into the Pacific ocean, without its resources being put to full use by anyone. Second, that
Columbia River Treaty while politicians talk, the time approaches more and more closely when the development of nuclear power will, as far at least as the United States is concerned, make the potential of this whole development entirely obsolete. We do not have time to wait. Third, that sale of downstream benefits generated within reach of markets in the United States is a lot more practical business than constructing a new high cost and high voltage transmission line 350 miles across some of the most rugged terrain on this continent to the B.C. lower mainland area, where there might be a market. Besides the Peace project, there are plenty of other untapped hydro resources within British Columbia which might be developed to satisfy the lower mainland market.
I think we neglect to understand that the power that is generated in the United States, the additional power as a result of the construction of these dams in Canada, is 350 miles across the heart of the Rocky mountains from any market within Canada. The construction of the necessary transmission lines across this terrain would be tremendous. Certainly this adds weight to the fact that when we are selling our downstream benefits we are doing something that is thoroughly and completely a good business proposition.
I was thoroughly perturbed at the implications I read into the speech of the leader of the New Democratic party, that because our friends in the United States profit from this bargain it cannot be a good thing for Canada. I suppose one can expect a socialist to have a mental block on the subject of profit, but the fact remains that such an argument is not only fallacious but it is mischievous, because it sows discord between two neighbours who should be friendly partners in developing this great enterprise. Any two persons who make a bargain do so only because each expects to profit from it. The better the bargain the more the profit that comes to each side.
I am very glad to know of the benefits that the United States will receive by way of power generation and particularly because of flood control as a result of this new arrangement. If it adds to the industrial prosperity of that nation, I am glad to know it. Just because United States benefits should not blind us to the fact that we benefit too. I am convinced that we have struck a good bargain, that we are getting the better of the deal, one which will benefit Canada in many ways other than just according to the specific terms of the treaty.
We are never going to build Canada by this niggardly approach that would rather make our own country poorer than allow any of our friends to gain a benefit from our own riches and good fortune. This is the dog in

Columbia River Treaty the manger attitude which holds Canada back both in its regional aspects and its international aspects. We are not going to make a great nation in Canada by curbing our imagination and enterprise and scrupulously rationing our existing poverty.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: Under a Liberal government.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext: There is wealth for all in this country if we will set ourselves to work with a will to develop it. I commend all who have had the foresight, imagination and energy to bring this project to its present stage and I assure them that this party will give them the utmost help in having the treaty finally approved in the most advantageous form to Canada by the present parliament in this present session.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the Columbia river treaty and the protocol are of much greater concern to the province of British Columbia than to the parliament of Canada.
Indeed, we of eastern Canada learned about British Columbia in our geography books many years ago, but we are much more familiar with the St. Lawrence river which flows from the great lakes through our province. Anyhow, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks on that treaty which, I feel, is most important for the development of natural resources in British Columbia.
In the white paper that was submitted to us a few days ago on the Columbia river treaty, I find this on page 128:
Background paper on the Columbia river treaty, 22 January 1964.
This is the background of this famous treaty:
In January 1961, the governments ot Canada and the United States signed the Columbia river treaty which envisaged co-operative development of the river on both sides of the border. The treaty was ratified shortly afterward by the United States congress. In Canada, however, ratification has not yet taken place.
This treaty was signed by the prime minister in 1961, when the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was prime minister of Canada.
In 1962, the Columbia river treaty was again brought up and also in 1963. There was, however, an aspect which had been forgotten by the Conservatives and which is, to my mind, the most important one, an essential one, and that is consultation with the province of British Columbia, so as to know how its prerogatives and autonomy would be safeguarded by any agreement or treaty that would be concluded between the United States and Canada.
The Conservative party has failed to recognize provincial autonomy, so much so that we have witnessed here, in this house, an imbroglio between the federal Conservative government and the government of Premier Bennett of British Columbia. In short, the Canadian government has taken it upon itself to conclude an agreement with the United States without even consulting with the province of British Columbia.
Last evening we heard an hon. member of the Conservative party attack this treaty. I feel that, in considering the ratification of this treaty, we should avoid playing politics.
I believe that this treaty protects fully and completely the rights of the province of British Columbia, since it is responsible for all the conditions, motives, reasons and other factors that make it possible to establish a better understanding between the provinces and Canada, while enabling Canada to reach an agreement with the United States.
In this I would not forgive myself if I did not heartily congratulate the premier of British Columbia, Mr. Bennett, for the position he took two years ago against the Conservative government, for the Conservative party did not recognize the autonomy of the province, its prerogatives and its rights in connection with the Columbia river.
Now, this treaty, Mr. Speaker, seems to arouse political interest within certain groups. In my opinion we should, as I said previously, put aside any question of political partisanship.
The Tories will try to suggest they could have settled the question in a more advantageous way, whereas we have proof that the present treaty is more advantageous than the one signed in 1961 by the government of the day.
Mr. Speaker, attempts will surely be made in British Columbia, especially among the socialists, including those in this house, to play politics with this treaty, by having the people of British Columbia believe that the economy of their province will be disrupted and, as the leader of the socialist party said last night, that the present federal government signed that treaty with British Columbia and the United States to satisfy the vanity of British Columbia's premier, Mr. Bennett.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that is an awful statement for the leader of the socialist party to make. I regret the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) is not here now, but I would remind him that the premier of British Columbia has done more in his province, within confederation, than the former premier of Saskatchewan could do for his province during 17 years, as far as economic growth and progress are concerned.

It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the treaty is not perfect and that it could be improved. However, I see no reason why it should not be approved since the natural resources in question are those of British Columbia.
In fact, when Ontario decides to export power to the United States, the Conservative government of that province insists on carrying out its business alone.
When Quebec exports iron ore from the Ungava to the United States the government of that province wishes to have a free hand, and now the situation is the same for the government of British Columbia whose efforts are seconded by the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) deserves nothing but congratulations at this time for the fine work he did in connection with the treaty.
I wish to point out that I am not a Liberal; far from it, I fight the Liberals. On the other hand, I am ready to acknowledge the efforts of the minister. The fact that British Columbia has a Social Credit government was no concern of his; he only saw in that treaty a measure that would contribute to the progress of British Columbia and Canada in general. He only saw the development of a potential likely to bring about an economic development such as British Columbia has never known in the past and will never enjoy in the future, thanks precisely to the harnessing of the Columbia river as a result of the treaty between British Columbia, Canada and the United States.
Mr. Speaker, there has been reference also to the financial angle, and it was said that the Canadian government was selling for a mess of pottage, its birthrights regarding the Columbia river. I do not believe that it is the only reason. On the contrary, I see in the Columbia river development tremendous opportunities for industrial development and for new industries in British Columbia.
We have received, from everywhere, comments, letters and telegrams. Some letters approved of the treaty, others were against it. However, everyone agrees on the need to really develop one's country, one's province.

Besides, it is a beautiful province, with a potential likely to result in a development that several provinces may never experience.

But the system advocated by Social Crediters is much more simple. And what we do not understand is why is it that in order to develop a river like the Columbia or any other natural resource in Canada, we have to get permission from foreign financial interests. And I draw the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to our suggestion.
If we have the men, the brains, the engineers, in short, all the materials to carry out the development of the Columbia river, why not use the Bank of Canada to create a credit equal to the potential that we can create with our arms, our brains and our physical efforts?

That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of the immediate development of the Chignecto complex through the harnessing of the bay of Fundy tides for power purposes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it seems appropriate that a notice of motion regarding the harnessing of the bay of Fundy tides should be debated at this juncture of the session, since we have before us today the treaty between Canada and the United States in connection with the development of the Columbia river from a power point of view. At the same time, we learned from the minister of northern affairs today that studies have been completed in connection with the Saint John river in New Brunswick and the Nelson river in Manitoba.
From a maritime point of view, the harnessing of the bay of Fundy tides is equivalent to the development of the Columbia river. It would produce an even greater amount of electrical energy if its full potential were exploited, and at a comparable mill rate. I intend to go into greater detail later in my speech on both of these aspects.
The unemployment statistics for the Atlantic provinces as of January 18, 1964, are the
[Mr. CaouetteJ
best indicator, if one is needed by the present government, that drastic measures must be adopted, measures of far more significance than any that have transpired in this regard since April 8, 1963.
Of the 466,000 individuals unemployed in Canada as of January 18, 1964, 72,000 were located in the Atlantic provinces, or 12.6 per cent of the labour force in that area. This is to be compared with the national level of 7 per cent or the rate in the prairies of 4.7 per cent and in Ontario of 4.9 per cent.
If further evidence is required of the crying need for bold and imaginative measures- terms which were favourites of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) when in opposition-it is supplied by a comparison of the average per capita income in the maritimes as compared with that in other parts of Canada. In Nova Scotia for the year 1962 it was $1,245, in New Brunswick, $1,107 and in Prince Edward Island, $1,009 as compared with a national average of close to $2,000.
The provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have vast wealth in natural resources. Nova Scotia has rich deposits of salt, gypsum and coal in great quantities. It has more than 10 million acres of forest land and 10 billion cubic feet of merchantable timber. New Brunswick has over 15 million acres of forest land and 17 billion cubic feet of merchantable timber. It has been recommended that the annual utilization of forest products could, and should, be doubled. New Brunswick also has large mineral deposits, some of which are in the development stage while others remain underdeveloped. The maritimes region should, and could, be the resource base for Britain and Europe and, with cheap and abundant power, could develop in processed products an important export trade served by its ports on a year round basis.
I was pleased to hear the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) say today, in reply to a question I posed, that an investigation from an engineering point of view is being undertaken by Foundation Engineering and would be completed in May. Unfortunately, this investigation appears to be confined to test borings which would provide little or no information pertaining to the earlier report presented to the government of the day relating to cost of construction and cost of power.
We have learned in recent days of further action taken by the government of the United States in connection with the development of Passamaquoddy bay from a power point of view. The cost of this project would be in the vicinity of $1 billion, a sum three times larger than that estimated as the cost of installing 50 units at both Shepody bay and Cumberland basin. I stated earlier in my

remarks that the power potential and mill rate for the Chignecto development compared favourably with the Columbia river development.
I should now like to read the report to the Chignecto canal committee by the Hon. Louis J. Robichaud, premier of the province of New Brunswick, on March 10, 1962. Premier Robichaud had this to say:
In December, 1961, the New Brunswick government retained the three highly qualified consulting firms H. G. Acres and Co. Ltd., Foundation of Canada Engineering Corporation Ltd., and LaSalle Hydraulic Laboratory Limited to prepare a joint preliminary report on the tidal power potential in the bay of Fundy.
Tlie highest tidal ranges in the world are known to exist at the head of the bay of Fundy. The following factors influenced the government of New Brunswick in having a preliminary study made of the tidal power potential in this area.
(1)	The rapidly increasing demand for electric power in the maritime provinces,
(2)	the increasing awareness of the beneficial effects which can accrue from interconnection of transmission systems on a provincial, national and international scale,
(3)	the stimulating effect which the availability of a large block of low-priced electrical energy would have on the expansion of primary industry in the region,
(4)	the possible effects which the development of tidal power at the head of the bay of Fundy might have on the Chignecto canal,
(5)	and the fact that development of the bulb turbine has improved the economics of tidal power.
The terms of reference to the consultants were limited to a re-examination of available information and engineering data and an assessment of tidal power feasibility in the light of present and future conditions. Special mention was made in the terms of reference to the Shepody-Cumberland tidal power sites.
In assessing the economics of the tidal power, three rates of interest were to be used:
(1)	2i per cent, which is the United States government interest rate for such projects;
(2)	5 per cent, which was approximately the current federal long term rate of interest;

The consulting firms were also asked to comment on the feasibility of a full scale engineering study of tidal power at the head of the bay of Fundy, and to include an estimate of the probable cost of such studies.
On January 15, the government of New Brunswick received the joint preliminary report entitled, "Appraisal of Tidal Power in the Bay of Fundy." I have pleasure in presenting a copy of this report to the Chignecto canal committee.
Following are the highlights of the report:
(1)	In appraising the possibilities of tidal power in the bay of Fundy, it was recognized that available site data was limited, and that additional field information must be obtained before detailed studies could be undertaken. The consultants advise, however, that they used generous contingency allowances and that conservative assumptions have been made in estimating the value of power and energy output obtainable.
(2)	Of the various possibilities for tidal power in the upper reaches of the Bay of Fundy, development of the Minas basin will be an undertaking of unprecedented magnitude and enormous energy potential. For example, if only one tenth of the

theoretical output could be utilized, it would represent some 15 million kilowatt hours per year of electrical energy. Of greater importance at the present time are the Shepody bay-Cumberland basin sites which offer a more immediate prospect of economic development.
(3)	Because of limited available information on foundation conditions, an arbitrary limitation of 50-9,000 kilowatt units was placed on each of the Cumberland and Shepody sites. The report is therefore based upon a total installation of 900.000 kw which available foundation data shows to be feasible. The installation might be increased to 200-9,000 kw units each if subsequent foundation exploration proved adequate. This means that as much as 3,600,000 kw might be installed following further engineering studies.
(4)	The preliminary estimate of capital cost for the total installation of 900,000 kw (450,000 kw each at the outlet of Shepody and Cumberland basin) amounts to $325,000,000, excluding interest during construction.
(5)	The preliminary studies show that 5.5 billion kwh per year could be generated from the 900,000 kw of installed capacity at the Cumberland-Shepody sites. More detailed system and hydraulic studies may result in a much larger output figure.
(6)	It was estimated that a minimum of 10 years would be required for preliminary exploration, design and construction of the Shepody-Cum-berland basin project. It was further estimated that at the present rate of load growth, the full output could be absorbed by New Brunswick and Nova Scotia within a five year period, provided that strong transmission interconnections with neighbouring utility systems are developed for power and energy interchange. Any industrial development in excess of past trends will allow the full output to be utilized at an even faster rate.
(7)	Using the criteria of interest rates as stated in the terms of reference, and using for depreciation purposes and assumed economic life of 50 years and one of 75 years, then the following are the estimated on-site energy costs from the Shepody-Cumberland tidal power development:
Assumed economic life-50 years: Shepody bay, 2h per cent interest rate, mills per kilowatt hour, 3.38; 35 per cent, 4.02; 5 per cent, 5.13.

The report states that it is not the intention to imply that these figures represent the lowest production costs which can be achieved. There is in fact, reason to believe that they could be reduced following more detailed study and economic analysis.
(8)	The consultants state that the development of the Shepody-Cumberland tidal sites would be feasible and would have a considerable impact on the economy of the maritime provinces. The development would be a continuing source of electrical energy, the cost of which would remain stable for a long period of time. It should be noted that conventional hydro developments and thermal generating plants will be needed in the maritimes as well as the tidal potential at the head of the bay of Fundy. Based upon a rate of growth similar to that of the past 20 years, it is

Chignecto Power Project
estimated that Nova Scotia and New Brunswick will require some 16.9 billion kilowatt hours of electrical energy by the year 1980. Indications are that with the availability of lower cost energy in large quantities, the rate of economic development and energy consumption will be increased.
(9)	For a number of years we have been interested in the improved transportation facilities for the maritime provinces which would result from the construction of the Chignecto canal. The joint preliminary report from the three consulting firms states that the construction of a dam across the entrance to the Cumberland basin, required for the development of tidal power and for keeping the water in this basin at a higher level, would have a beneficial effect on the cost and operation of the approach to the Chignecto canal by reducing the initial cost of dredging, as well as its future maintenance costs. It would also reduce the tidal currents now prevailing in the Cumberland basin, thus improving the navigation.
In answering a part of the terms of reference given to the three consulting firms, they state the following:
"It is considered that further study of the various sites for tidal power development at the head of the bay of Fundy, and in particular, the Shepody bay and Cumberland basin sites, is justified. It is therefore recommended that studies and investigation be carried out as outlined. The costs given for each item should be regarded as an estimate:
Phase I
Field surveys, including foundation borings, preliminary engineering design, and system studies, $573,000.
Phase II

Total studies and survey, $2 million."
I am pleased to present this report to the Chignecto canal committee. I would appreciate it if you would give it careful consideration because I believe that it provides the technical background upon which more detailed studies and planning may be developed and around which the economy of the Atlantic region may be transformed.
Mr. Speaker, that, as I said, is a report given to the Chignecto canal committee by the premier of the province of New Brunswick. As all members of this house know, the premier of the province of New Brunswick is a Liberal, as is the government of the day in Ottawa. I recommend to the government his conclusions from this study and urge them to take immediate steps to speed up the investigations being carried out into the potential of the Chignecto complex, in the hope that they will find the answer to the problem of the Atlantic area, a problem of which we are all aware, a problem we are all endeavouring to solve. I hope that upon the conclusion of their investigations into this very important project we will find a positive step which can be taken for the construction of the dam that will revitalize the economy of the Atlantic area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to commend the hon. member who has just introduced this resolution. This matter has been one of great concern and discussion over many years in the maritime provinces. I know it is of very great interest to his particular area and I think this interest is shared by other parts of Atlantic Canada. Like any other project that will benefit the Atlantic area, I am sure that those in this house, such as myself, who represent areas in the Atlantic provinces will for the most part support the general intention of this motion and the project, although we have some reservations about the feasibility and many other practical aspects of the proposed development. Until further studies are completed I find it difficult to make a complete decision or pass judgment on the undertaking.
There is however, Mr. Speaker, one important reservation that I wish to make personally as far as supporting the motion is concerned. I would be very strongly opposed to any action on the Chignecto project that would interefere with or delay in any way the construction of the Northumberland causeway connecting Prince Edward Island and the mainland of Canada at a point in New Brunswick. It is my opinion-and I am sure it is shared by many hon. members in the house; by all islanders, of course, and many other people in the Atlantic provinces-that there is a great urgency and need for the construction of the causeway and that this should be undertaken before any other major developments of a similar nature in the Atlantic area.
Having made the position clear, Mr. Speaker, that the Prince Edward Island causeway must be given top priority in every consideration, we are certainly not opposed to anything that would benefit the Atlantic provinces; and I am sure that the Chignecto development, if and when it is found feasible, will be of very real benefit to nearly all that area. However, I feel that because of the more urgent need and the commitments which have already been given, the causeway should receive top priority. On the day on which this house dissolved before the election in 1962 the prime minister of the day, the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), announced that the Northumberland causeway would be built.

In fact, he elaborated on this to a considerable extent, to indicate the length of time it would take to construct the causeway, the number of men required and the estimated cost involved. This was a definite commitment by the prime minister of that time and it was accepted as such without reservation. The present government has confirmed this commitment, and as soon as the studies are completed, which we hope will be very soon, we would expect this project to get under way. As I say, Mr. Speaker, we would be strongly opposed to any other development which would interfere with that undertaking in any way, and we cannot overlook the possibility that proceeding with Chignecto would interfere substantially with construction of the causeway.
The hon. member's motion for the development of the Chignecto complex reads in this way:
That...the government should give consideration to the advisability of immediate development of the Chignecto complex through the harnessing of the bay of Fundy tides for power purposes.
I believe that this motion for the immediate development of the Chignecto complex is probably premature in view of the fact that detailed studies have not been completed with regard to the feasibility of such a project.
The preliminary report made to the government of New Brunswick, which the hon. member quoted extensively, is entitled "Appraisal of the tidal power of the bay of Fundy". The number one highlight of the report reads as follows:
In appraising the possibilities of tidal power in the bay of Fundy, it was recognized that available site data was limited and that additional field information must be obtained before detailed studies could be undertaken.
Then the report indicates that this information is necessary before detailed studies can be made, and certainly we cannot consider construction of the project until the studies are completed.
In replying this afternoon to question No. 56, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) indicated that the final preliminary report would be made on May 31 next. I think that any consideration of this matter should be left until that report is available. Although the motion requests the government to give immediate consideration to the Chignecto development for power purposes, the promoter speaks of the development as the Chignecto complex. I presume he has in mind-and he makes reference to this in his report-a canal, as well as the power aspects of the project. In this connection I believe that, even if we view the project generously, in no way can it be established that there is any justifiable or reasonable relation between the benefits
Chignecto Power Project which would accrue from this undertaking and the costs involved. The costs have been estimated at $140 million. Taking interest on that amount at 5 per cent per annum, and operation and maintenance costs, that would mean an annual total cost of $10 million. The shipping benefits are estimated at $500,000, which would mean a net figure of $9.5 million a year.
It has been suggested that construction of the canal would lead to a large industrial development, but no definite commitment or information as to the nature of this complex has been forthcoming. It has also been suggested that shipping through the proposed canal would mean a considerable saving of shipping time; but when we take into account the time that is lost in passing through 19 miles of canals and locks, it is doubtful whether very much time could actually be saved. There is also the problem of fog which could greatly delay shipping. So I submit it is dubious how much actual shipping time would be saved by using a canal in preference to the present transportation route.
On the power aspects of the project, Mr. Speaker, I think there is the misconception- the report does make some reference to this- that the canal would provide water for power development; that it would assist in some way which the hon. member mentioned. I do not think it would be of very substantial benefit in assisting power development; at least, the water would not be used to produce power.
There is no reason to believe, then, that any great power benefits would be derived from construction of the canal. Studies are presently under way to determine the feasibility of constructing a dam across the bay, and the building of a powerhouse. I believe this is also mentioned in the report which has been read; paragraph 3 has to do with surveying the foundations. The estimated cost is between $350 and $400 million. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that until these studies are completed any consideration of this very worthwhile project should be postponed.
I hope that what I have said has not conveyed the impression that I am opposed to the construction of the Chignecto complex, particularly the power aspects of it. I think very serious consideration should be given to the construction of a canal, but I do not think it will be of any practical benefit. In fact, if anything I think it will be a loss. However, I support, and I know all those who represent areas in the maritime provinces support, this project. We hope the studies under way will prove it is feasible, and that it can be built at reasonable cost. I further hope that after the Northumberland causeway is constructed, construction will begin on the Chignecto complex.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the comments which I have to make concerning the motion moved by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) are fairly brief. I appreciate that this motion with regard to this possible construction is something which has been talked about a good deal, both in our developments in the Atlantic provinces and also in this house. I cannot help but recall that another quite important project, the Passamaquoddy development, has been mentioned here recently. There is presently a bill before the U.S. congress which would bring about study and consideration of the Passamaquoddy project. I should like to draw a comparison between the Passamaquoddy and the harnessing of the tides at the upper end of the bay of Fundy, because there is a degree of similarity between them. While I would not say anything against the development of the Passamaquoddy I do think certain advantages are to be derived by Canada from the development of the tides at the upper end of the bay of Fundy which do not exist to the same extent in the case of the Passamaquoddy development.
In the first place, the tides at the upper end of the bay of Fundy are very much higher than at the lower end of the Passamaquoddy. I think it is true to say that there is a rise and fall twice a day of something like 40 feet of water at the upper end of the bay of Fundy, which impounds a tremendous volume of water somewhere. It staggers the imagination to think what might be done if that were harnessed so that there could be a high level reservoir and a low level reservoir, and all the other constructions about which I must confess, not being an engineer, I am unable to enlighten the house. Yet they impress us all with the general idea that there is a great body and volume of power there which might possibly be harnessed to the advantage of this country.
It is very important, as the previous speaker said, that today we should have had the announcement from the Minister of Transport, speaking for the Atlantic development board, that the Foundation of Canada Engineering have been retained to make a survey and to make actual borings and that sort of thing. I am sure that is very interesting and, not only that, but it is very encouraging to all of us who are very much interested in these developments.
I think it might be considered that the operation is under way and I was greatly interested, in listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) when he read from the prepared report as presented by the premier of New Brunswick in which it was considered that New Brunswick and Nova Scotia could absorb this large
[Mr. Mullally.1
volume of power in a matter of five years. It seems to be difficult to visualize, but nevertheless that could be a possibility, and I suggest that it also brings to mind this fact, that when a development of this nature is carried on and it becomes a reality, and the power becomes available, then it is one of the most impressive and most important protections against inflation that any country could possibly have; because the capital cost has been incurred and has been provided for, and from then on the maintenance is very low. That point might have some bearing when this matter is being considered.
I also find the decision of the government of a few years ago, and the government of today, that any power surplus to our needs might very well be exported, and with some advantage to ourselves, lends itself again to the general idea of the development of the tides in the upper bay of Fundy, because it is only something like 100 miles to the state of Maine border and, presumably, access to a New England grid system, and we are told that they need power and they need it quite badly.
Another advantage of this development in the upper end of the bay of Fundy as compared with Passamaquoddy, is the factor that there is no effect on the fisheries and the fishing industry to be considered in connection with it; and so I am pleased, and I congratulate the hon. member for Cumberland for bringing this matter before the attention of the house.
I am one of those who think that the question of inflation is very important, one which we cannot afford to ignore. It is just as sure as the air we breathe that we are in for a degree of inflation year after year. That has been the history of the past and I have no doubt that it will be the history of the future. This is one way in which protection may be provided against inflation so far as electrical energy costs are concerned, because they have been pretty well frozen at the point of present costs, with money rates as they are now.
So, Mr. Speaker, I have nothing more to. add, except to lend my voice in support of the motion that has been moved and brought to the attention of hon. members, and I have great pleasure in seconding it.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to make only a few general remarks in connection with this motion moved by the hon. member for Cumberland. My remarks will be based first on the very general topic of financing. It would seem to me that when we are talking about these large developments we must be concerned about the financing of any projects of this nature.

I certainly want to go on record as being one who feels that any development anywhere in Canada, whether it be power or any other type of development is certainly something which is most welcome. We believe that power development, of course, is a very important part of life in Canada and the world, and we believe that it is time now for action on any type of development that has to do with waterpower.
We have often heard the expression used that we are heading into a day of atomic energy development, which it is said is going to come into competition with hydro development. One of the reasons that we in the province of British Columbia have facing us in the next eight years, power development the cost of which would run well in excess of a billion dollars-as a matter of fact $1,200,000,000-is because of the fact that we are confronted with a situation in which we must make these developments at the earliest possible date.
We recognize the situation that was referred to by the last speaker, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming), in that the gradual reduction of the purchasing power of the dollar seems to be something that we cannot escape. Once the hydro development is built and in operation, even if the cost to the consumer can be held over a period of years at the same price, then if we continue dividing the dollar we are not going to have a continual reduction in the cost of that power. I am all in favour of the development of power wherever it can be undertaken in Canada, but I do think there are a few things we should keep in mind in connection with this. First of all, as I have said, there is the question of financing. In the province of British Columbia the B.C. government is prepared to go all the way on the development of the Peace river and also the Columbia river power projects.
We have a motion before us, if I read it correctly, which suggests the immediate development of the Chigneeto complex through the harnessing of the bay of Fundy tides for power purposes, and it suggests to me that the financing is going to be on a Canada-wide basis. I am not sure whether this is true, as I was not here when the hon. member introduced the motion; but if this is the case I think we should have no objection other than this, that it must be a fiscal arrangement between the provinces and the dominion government in which it is well understood by the provincial governments and the federal government that these arrangements are going to be made.
Now, to isolate one part of Canada from another is neither right nor possible. We who are living in British Columbia are in one of
Chigneeto Power Project the most advantageous provinces, as far as making a living is concerned, and as far as progress is concerned, that there is in the whole of the Dominion of Canada.
Where there are provinces and communities not as well off as we are, we certainly recognize that we are all Canadians and that assistance must be forthcoming. But let this be done through the proper channels of negotiation, so that we will know what the charges and the burden on other people are going to be.
The word "inflation" is used quite freely from time to time, but I wonder whether we are using the right word when we do so because, as I have said before, when one considers the purchasing power of the dollar in relation to the hours of work required to buy a particular article, the situation is no different now from what it was 50 years ago. I used this illustration on another occasion. In the late 1800's my father had to work two days in order to be able to buy a pair of hand-sewn cowboy boots. In the cattle country around the Williams lake area today an individual can go and buy a pair of cowboy boots with the proceeds of two days work. There is not too much difference. But to those people who are on fixed incomes the lessening of the purchasing power of the dollar becomes very real. So I think we should possibly coin a new phrase for what I call the dividing of the dollar.
Finally, I want to assure those in the mari-times that I support fully any type of development that can be reasonably undertaken in any part of Canada, including the good provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and the other maritime provinces. I think it is good that we should look at development in Canada on a broad base so that all Canadians can benefit and I have in mind the total development of hydroelectric power. The provision of a national grid from coast to coast so that power can flow one way or the other as need may arise is a development for the not too distant future. With these few remarks I give my assurance to my hon. friends from the maritimes that we are completely in favour of any development we can have in Canada, including the maritimes.

Mr. Speaker,
I am very happy to have the opportunity to participate in the discussion of this notice of motion. For very many years the tides of the Fundy have been a matter of speculation and great interest to people concerned with the generation of electrical power. In the past the tides have been a problem. Indeed, they have created very many economic problems for various areas along both sides of the bay of Fundy. But many have looked forward to the

Chignecto Power Project time when the tides of the Fundy could be harnessed for the benefit of mankind and thus bring power to this region in great quantities. Whether or not this time has yet come is indeed a very good question.
I was somewhat surprised that the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) did not consider to any extent at all the possible repercussions of tidal power development at the present time on the use of coal for the generation of power. While I, like the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming), am not an engineer and therefore not as cognizant of the intricacies of these problems as one would wish to be, nevertheless I would hope that before the government would see fit to go ahead with the development of power from the tides of the Fundy every avenue of research would be explored for the purpose of finding a method of developing power economically through the use of Nova Scotia coal. Indeed, at a time when there is talk in the newspapers of the possibility of the opening of a new coal mine right in the constituency of the hon. member for Cumberland, and at a time when the coal of Cape Breton is not being utilized to the degree it could be,
I think the development of power from coal and a means of making such generation of power more economical should have first priority.
Having said that, I hasten to associate myself with the comments of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, that when tidal development is being considered it should be kept in mind that the areas at the head of the bay of Fundy have a very distinct advantage over the Passamaquoddy project, inasmuch as there would be very little effect, if any, upon the fisheries. Because of the high tides and the constant agitation of the water there the fishing industry has never developed nor, indeed, does that area have the potential for fishing that the area at the other end of the bay of Fundy has, which would be affected by the Passamaquoddy project.
I was surprised to find that in considering tidal development at the head of the bay of Fundy the hon. member for Cumberland had an obvious preference for the Shepody bay project, which would lie entirely in New Brunswick and which would appear not to have nearly the potential for tidal power development of the Minas basin. In addition, of course, the Minas basin project would bring great benefit to the Parrsboro area.

If I may, I should like to continue the remarks I was making before I was interrupted by the backbenchers on the Conservative side. I am sorry if I in any way misquoted the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates). What I intended to say was, and I repeat, that the whole Chignecto complex would include the canal, while the hon. member seemed to stress particularly the development at the head of Shepody bay rather than the Minas basin development. I would point out that the Minas basin development would generate a great deal more power. In addition, it would solve the problem of transportation from the Annapolis valley to the Parrsboro area and would open the way for great economic advancement in the Parrsboro area which is situated in the hon. member's constituency. I was surprised, therefore, to find him prejudiced against the Minas basin development.
Turning to the question of whether or not the entire Chignecto complex development should be considered, I would say that it would appear to me this resoultion is an attempt by the hon. member to have the Chignecto canal, which is an entirely separate consideration from the standpoint of the development of tidal power, given consideration at this time. There are different considerations and different points of view in connection with these two projects. There are many people who, while they are in favour of the tidal power development, if and when this can be done without harming the use of coal for power generation in the maritimes, have very serious doubts as to whether the Chignecto canal project is an economic or worth-while one in relation to the amount of money that would have to be expended.
The Minas basin power development would generate 15 billion kilowatt hours per year. Certainly, this would provide us with the amount of power that would be necessary for the industrial needs of the area for some time to come. I would, in general, agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Mullally) who said that the causeway to
Chignecto Power Project Prince Edward Island should take precedence over this power development. This point is well taken, indeed.
In conclusion I would only want to say that for many years man has been interested in the development of new and more economic means for the development of power. Many years ago in my constituency of Halifax there was a gentleman by the name of Parsons, whose first name escapes me, who carried on extensive experiments in connection with the generation of power from waves. Actually, his experiments had advanced to the point where he was able to light a small house with electricity from power developed with an apparatus for the generation of power from waves. There are many ways in which power can be developed. I think the notice of motion put on the order paper for the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) is one that will, in years to come, deserve much attention.
